en: Saṃyutta Nikāya 46.1 Himavanta Sutta: The Himalayas Chapter 1: The Section on Mountains Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, just as the Himalayas, the king of mountains, is the chief among mountains, so too, among all forms of asceticism, the asceticism of the Tathāgata is the chief. And what, bhikkhus, is the asceticism of the Tathāgata? Here, bhikkhus, the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, has abandoned the underlying tendency to lust for sensual pleasures, has eradicated it, and has made an end of it; he has abandoned the underlying tendency to aversion, has eradicated it, and has made an end of it; he has abandoned the underlying tendency to views, has eradicated it, and has made an end of it; he has abandoned the underlying tendency to doubt, has eradicated it, and has made an end of it; he has abandoned the underlying tendency to conceit, has eradicated it, and has made an end of it; he has abandoned the underlying tendency to desire for existence, has eradicated it, and has made an end of it; he has abandoned ignorance, has eradicated it, and has made an end of it. This, bhikkhus, is called the asceticism of the Tathāgata. Among all forms of asceticism, this asceticism of the Tathāgata is the chief.”
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
"Bhikkhus, just as, depending on Himavā, the king of mountains, elephants increase their bodies and acquire strength;
and having increased their bodies and acquired strength there, they descend into small ponds; and having descended into the small ponds, [they descend] into great ponds..."
They flow into the great pools; having flowed into the great pools, they flow into the small streams; having flowed into the small streams, they flow into the great rivers;
having flowed into the great rivers, they flow into the great ocean, the sea. There they attain greatness and abundance in their physical form.

In the same way, monks, a monk—relying on virtue, established in virtue—develops the seven factors of awakening and cultivates the seven factors of awakening, thereby attaining greatness and abundance in regard to the teachings.

And how, monks, does a monk, relying on virtue and established in virtue, develop the seven factors of enlightenment and cultivate them repeatedly so that he attains greatness and abundance in these qualities?
Here, monks, a monk develops the mindfulness factor of enlightenment, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment;
he develops the investigation-of-phenomena factor of enlightenment... [and so forth].
He develops the enlightenment factor of energy …pe… he develops the enlightenment factor of rapture …pe… he develops the enlightenment factor of tranquility …pe…
“He develops the enlightenment factor of concentration … [and so on] … he develops the enlightenment factor of equanimity, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation,

and results in relinquishment. It is in this way, monks, that a monk, by relying on virtue and being established in virtue, develops the seven factors of enlightenment and cultivates them repeatedly, thereby attaining greatness and abundance in the qualities.”

The Discourse on the Body. The setting was at Sāvatthī.
"Bhikkhus, just as this body is sustained by nutriment, it persists dependent upon nutriment; without nutriment, it does not persist."
In the same way, monks, the five hindrances persist by means of nutriment; they persist dependent on nutriment, and they do not persist without nutriment.
And what, monks, is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen sensual desire, or for the increase, expansion, and abundance of arisen sensual desire?
There is, monks, the sign of the beautiful.
In this regard, frequent improper attention is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen sensual desire, or for the increase and expansion of arisen sensual desire.
And what, monks, is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen ill will, or for the increase and expansion of arisen ill will?
There is, monks, the sign of repulsion.
Therein, the frequent practice of improper attention is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen ill will, or for the increase and expansion of arisen ill will.
And what, monks, is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen sloth and torpor, or for the increase and expansion of arisen sloth and torpor?
There is, monks, discontent, drowsiness, yawning, lethargy after eating, and mental sluggishness.
Therein, the frequent practice of improper attention—this is the nutriment.
This is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen sloth and torpor, or for the increase and expansion of sloth and torpor once they have arisen.
And what, monks, is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen restlessness and remorse, or for the increase and expansion of restlessness and remorse once they have arisen?
There is, monks, the lack of tranquility of mind.
In this regard, frequent improper attention is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen restlessness and remorse, and for the increase and expansion of arisen restlessness and remorse.
And what, monks, is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen doubt, and for the increase and expansion of arisen doubt?
“There are, monks, things that are a basis for doubt.
Therein, the frequent practice of improper attention is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen doubt, or for the increase, expansion, and proliferation of arisen doubt.”
“Just as, monks, this body is sustained by nutriment, persists in dependence on nutriment, and does not persist without nutriment;
even so, monks, these five hindrances are sustained by nutriment, persist in dependence on nutriment, and do not persist without nutriment.
Just as, monks, this body is sustained by nutriment, persists in dependence on nutriment, and does not persist without nutriment;”
In the same way, monks, the seven factors of awakening are sustained by nutriment; they persist in dependence on nutriment and do not persist without nutriment.
And what, monks, is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen mindfulness factor of awakening, or for the development and fulfillment of the arisen mindfulness factor of awakening?
There are, monks, phenomena conducive to the mindfulness factor of awakening.

In this regard, frequent application of wise attention is the nutriment for the arising of the enlightenment factor of mindfulness that has not yet arisen, or for the development and fulfillment of the enlightenment factor of mindfulness that has already arisen.

And what, monks, is the nutriment for the arising of the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena that has not yet arisen, or for the development and fulfillment of the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena that has already arisen?
"There are, monks, wholesome and unwholesome states, blameworthy and blameless states, inferior and superior states, and dark and bright states that contrast with one another.

In this regard, frequent and systematic attention is the requisite for the arising of the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena that has not yet arisen, or for the development and fulfillment of the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena that has already arisen."
"And what, monks, is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of energy, or for the fulfillment by development of the arisen enlightenment factor of energy?
There is, monks, the element of initiative, the element of exertion, and the element of perseverance.
In that regard, there is frequent application of wise attention."
This nutriment leads to the arising of the unarisen factor of energy-enlightenment, or to the development and fulfillment of the arisen factor of energy-enlightenment.
And what, monks, is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen factor of rapture-enlightenment, or for the development and fulfillment of the arisen factor of rapture-enlightenment?
There are, monks, states that are the basis for the factor of rapture-enlightenment.
In this regard, frequent application of wise attention is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen factor of rapture, or for the development and fulfillment of the arisen factor of rapture.
And what, bhikkhus, is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen factor of tranquility, or for the development and fulfillment of the arisen factor of tranquility?
There is, monks, tranquility of body and tranquility of mind.

In that regard, frequent application of wise attention is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of tranquility, and for the fulfillment by development of the arisen enlightenment factor of tranquility.
"And what, monks, is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of concentration, or for the fulfillment by development of the arisen enlightenment factor of concentration?
There is, monks, the sign of serenity and the sign of non-distraction.
In this regard, the frequent practice of wise attention [is the nutriment]."
This nutriment leads to the arising of the unarisen factor of enlightenment that is concentration, or to the development and fulfillment of the arisen factor of enlightenment that is concentration.

And what, monks, is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen factor of enlightenment that is equanimity, or for the development and fulfillment of the arisen factor of enlightenment that is equanimity?
There are, monks, phenomena conducive to the factor of enlightenment that is equanimity.

In this regard, frequent application of wise attention is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of equanimity, and for the development and fulfillment of the arisen enlightenment factor of equanimity. Just as, monks, this body is sustained by nutriment, persists in dependence on nutriment, and does not persist without nutriment; so too, monks, the enlightenment factor of equanimity is sustained by nutriment, persists in dependence on nutriment, and does not persist without nutriment. What is its nutriment? Frequent application of wise attention is its nutriment. Thus, monks, the enlightenment factor of equanimity is sustained by nutriment, persists in dependence on nutriment, and does not persist without nutriment. The Discourse on Virtue “Bhikkhus, those bhikkhus who are perfected in virtue, perfected in concentration, perfected in wisdom, perfected in liberation, and perfected in the knowledge and vision of liberation—to seeing them, I say, bhikkhus, is of great benefit.”
“Monks, I say that listening to them is very helpful for those monks;
I say that approaching them is very helpful for those monks;
I say that attending upon them is very helpful for those monks.”
"Bhikkhus, I say that recollection is of great benefit to those bhikkhus;
I say that going forth after them is also of great benefit to those bhikkhus. And why is that?"
“Bhikkhus, having heard the Dhamma from such bhikkhus, one dwells withdrawn by means of a twofold withdrawal: withdrawal of body and withdrawal of mind.
Dwelling thus withdrawn, one recollects and reflects upon that Dhamma.
On whatever occasion, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwelling thus withdrawn recollects and reflects upon that Dhamma, on that occasion the mindfulness enlightenment factor is aroused in that bhikkhu.”
At that time, the bhikkhu develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness;
at that time, the enlightenment factor of mindfulness reaches fulfillment through development in the bhikkhu.
Dwelling thus mindful, he investigates, examines, and scrutinizes that phenomenon with wisdom.
“Bhikkhus, on whatever occasion a bhikkhu, dwelling thus mindfully, investigates, examines, and applies close scrutiny to that phenomenon with wisdom,
on that occasion the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena is aroused in that bhikkhu;
on that occasion the bhikkhu develops the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena.”
At that time, the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena reaches fulfillment through development for the bhikkhu.
As he investigates, scrutinizes, and examines that phenomenon with wisdom, his energy becomes aroused and unflagging.
Monks, at whatever time a bhikkhu investigates, scrutinizes, and examines that phenomenon with wisdom...
Energy is aroused and unflagging; on that occasion, the enlightenment factor of energy is aroused for the bhikkhu;
on that occasion, the bhikkhu develops the enlightenment factor of energy; on that occasion, the enlightenment factor of energy reaches fulfillment through development for the bhikkhu.
For one who has aroused energy, spiritual rapture arises that is not worldly.
Monks, at whatever time spiritual rapture arises for a monk who has aroused energy, at that time the factor of enlightenment consisting of rapture is initiated in that monk;
at that time the monk develops the factor of enlightenment consisting of rapture.
At that time, the factor of enlightenment that is rapture reaches fulfillment through development for the bhikkhu.
When one’s mind is filled with rapture, the body becomes tranquil and the mind also becomes tranquil.
Bhikkhus, at whatever time the body of a bhikkhu whose mind is filled with rapture becomes tranquil and the mind also becomes tranquil—
At that time, the factor of enlightenment of tranquility has been undertaken by the bhikkhu;
at that time, the bhikkhu develops the factor of enlightenment of tranquility; at that time, the factor of enlightenment of tranquility reaches the fulfillment of its development for the bhikkhu.
When the body is tranquil and he is happy, his mind becomes concentrated.
“Bhikkhus, at whatever time a bhikkhu’s mind becomes concentrated when his body is tranquil and he is happy, at that time the enlightenment factor of concentration is initiated in that bhikkhu;
at that time the bhikkhu develops the enlightenment factor of concentration;
at that time the enlightenment factor of concentration reaches fulfillment by development in that bhikkhu.”
Thus he thoroughly looks on with equanimity at the mind so well-concentrated.

Bhikkhus, at whatever time a bhikkhu thoroughly looks on with equanimity at the mind so well-concentrated, at that time the enlightenment factor of equanimity is aroused in that bhikkhu; at that time the enlightenment factor of equanimity...
At that time, a bhikkhu develops the factor of enlightenment of equanimity; at that time, the factor of enlightenment of equanimity reaches fulfillment through development for that bhikkhu.
When, monks, these seven factors of enlightenment have been developed and frequently practiced in this way, seven fruits and seven benefits are to be expected.
What are the seven fruits and seven benefits?
One attains final knowledge early in this very life.
If one does not attain final knowledge early in this very life, then one attains it at the time of death.

If one does not attain final knowledge early in this very life, nor at the time of death, then, with the total destruction of the five lower fetters, one becomes one who attains nibbāna in the interval.
If he does not attain final knowledge early in this very life, nor does he attain final knowledge at the time of death,
nor does he become one who attains Nibbāna in the interval through the total destruction of the five lower fetters,
then he becomes one who attains Nibbāna upon landing through the total destruction of the five lower fetters.
If he does not attain final knowledge in this very life, nor at the time of death,
nor by the total destruction of the five lower fetters become one who attains nibbāna in the interval,
nor by the total destruction of the five lower fetters become one who attains nibbāna upon landing, then—
With the total destruction of the five lower fetters, one becomes one who attains final nibbāna without exertion.
If one does not attain final knowledge prematurely in this very life, nor attain final knowledge at the time of death,
nor become one who attains final nibbāna in the interval through the total destruction of the five lower fetters, [then...]
With the total destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one who attains nibbāna upon landing;
or, if not one who attains nibbāna upon landing with the total destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one who attains nibbāna without exertion;
or, if not one who attains nibbāna without exertion with the total destruction of the five lower fetters, then he becomes one who attains nibbāna with exertion.
If he does not attain final knowledge in this very life, nor at the time of death,
nor through the total destruction of the five lower fetters become one who attains nibbāna in the interval,

nor through the total destruction of the five lower fetters become one who attains nibbāna upon landing... [nor through the total destruction of the five lower fetters become one who attains nibbāna without exertion...]
With the complete destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one who attains final nibbāna without exertion;
or, if not one who attains final nibbāna without exertion with the complete destruction of the five lower fetters,
then he becomes one who goes upstream, bound for the Akaniṭṭha realm.

At one time, the Venerable Sāriputta was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There, the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the bhikkhus:
"Friends, bhikkhus.
"Friend," those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Sāriputta.
The Venerable Sāriputta said this:
"Friends, there are these seven factors of enlightenment.
Which seven?"

The mindfulness enlightenment factor, the investigation-of-dhammas enlightenment factor, the energy enlightenment factor, the rapture enlightenment factor, the tranquility enlightenment factor, the concentration enlightenment factor,
and the equanimity enlightenment factor— these, friends, are the seven enlightenment factors.
Of these seven enlightenment factors, friends, whichever enlightenment factor I wish to dwell in during the morning session, in that very enlightenment factor I dwell during the morning session.
By whichever factor of enlightenment I desire to dwell during the midday period, by that very factor of enlightenment I dwell during the midday period;
by whichever factor of enlightenment I desire to dwell during the evening period, by that very factor of enlightenment I dwell during the evening period.
If, friends, the mindfulness factor of enlightenment is present in me, it occurs to me: "It is immeasurable," and it occurs to me: "It is well undertaken"; and as it persists, I know: "It persists."
Even if it subsides in me, I understand: ‘It is due to this specific condition that it subsides in me. ... [as before] ...
If, friends, there is the enlightenment factor of equanimity in me, I know: ‘It is immeasurable,’ I know: ‘It is well undertaken,’ and while it persists, I understand:
‘It persists. Even if it subsides in me, I understand: ‘It is due to this specific condition that it subsides in me.’
"Suppose, friends, a king or a royal minister had a chest full of various colored garments.
Whatever pair of garments he might wish to put on in the morning, that very pair of garments he would put on in the morning;
whatever pair of garments he might wish to put on at midday, that very pair of garments he would put on at midday."
Whatever pair of robes one might wish to put on in the evening, that very pair of robes one would put on in the evening.
In the same way, friend, whichever of these seven factors of awakening I wish to dwell in during the morning, with that very factor of awakening I dwell in the morning;
whichever factor of awakening I wish to dwell in at midday, with that very factor of awakening I dwell in at midday.

By whichever factor of enlightenment I desire to dwell during the evening, by that very factor of enlightenment I dwell during the evening. If, friends, the mindfulness factor of enlightenment is present to me, it occurs to me: "It is immeasurable," it occurs to me: "It is well undertaken," and as it persists, I know: "It persists. Even if it should fade away from me, I know: "It fades away from me due to this specific condition" ... [and so on for the remaining factors] ... ... If, friends, the investigation-of-states factor of enlightenment is present to me, it occurs to me: "It is immeasurable," it occurs to me: "It is well undertaken," and as it persists, I know: "It persists. Even if it should fade away from me, I know: "It fades away from me due to this specific condition. Even if it should fade away from me, I know: "It fades away from me due to this specific condition. If, friends, the tranquility factor of enlightenment is present to me, it occurs to me: "It is immeasurable," it occurs to me: "It is well undertaken," and as it persists, I know: "It persists. Even if it should fade away from me, I know: "It fades away from me due to this specific condition. Even if it should fade away from me, I know: "It fades away from me due to this specific condition. Friends, these seven factors of enlightenment are developed and cultivated in such a way that they lead to the realization of the fruit of arahantship, to the realization of the fruit of non-returning, to the realization of the fruit of once-returning, and to the realization of the fruit of stream-entry. What seven? The mindfulness factor of enlightenment, the investigation-of-states factor of enlightenment, the energy factor of enlightenment, the rapture factor of enlightenment, the tranquility factor of enlightenment, the concentration factor of enlightenment, and the equanimity factor of enlightenment. Friends, these seven factors of enlightenment are developed and cultivated in such a way that they lead to the realization of the fruit of arahantship, to the realization of the fruit of non-returning, to the realization of the fruit of once-returning, and to the realization of the fruit of stream-entry. Friends, these four foundations of mindfulness are developed and cultivated in such a way that they lead to the realization of the fruit of arahantship, to the realization of the fruit of non-returning, to the realization of the fruit of once-returning, and to the realization of the fruit of stream-entry. What four? Here, friends, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world; he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... he dwells contemplating mind in mind... he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. Friends, these four foundations of mindfulness are developed and cultivated in such a way that they lead to the realization of the fruit of arahantship, to the realization of the fruit of non-returning, to the realization of the fruit of once-returning, and to the realization of the fruit of stream-entry. Friends, these four right strivings are developed and cultivated in such a way that they lead to the realization of the fruit of arahantship, to the realization of the fruit of non-returning, to the realization of the fruit of once-returning, and to the realization of the fruit of stream-entry. What four? Here, friends, a bhikkhu generates desire for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states; he makes an effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives. On one occasion the Blessed One was staying at Sāketa in the Añjana Grove, the Deer Park.
Then the wanderer Kuṇḍaliya approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the wanderer Kuṇḍaliya said this to the Blessed One:
“Master Gotama, I am one who dwells in a monastery and frequents assemblies.
After my meal, having finished my breakfast, Master Gotama, this is my custom:
I walk and wander from monastery to monastery and from park to park.”
"Therefore, I see some recluses and brahmins there speaking about the benefits of liberation through traditional doctrines and the benefits of finding fault [with others], saying:
'But what benefit does Master Gotama dwell in?
" "The Tathāgata, Kuṇḍaliya, dwells for the benefit of the fruit of true knowledge and liberation," [he replied].
“But which phenomena, Master Gotama, when developed and cultivated, fulfill true knowledge and liberation?
“The seven factors of enlightenment, Kuṇḍaliya, when developed and cultivated, fulfill true knowledge and liberation.
“But which phenomena, Master Gotama, when developed and cultivated, fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment?”
“Kundaliya, the four foundations of mindfulness, when developed and cultivated, fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment.
“But, Master Gotama, which phenomena, when developed and cultivated, fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness?
“Kundaliya, the three kinds of good conduct, when developed and cultivated, fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness.”
“But, Master Gotama, what things, when developed and cultivated, fulfill the three types of good conduct?
“Restraint of the sense faculties, Kuṇḍaliya, when developed and cultivated, fulfills the three types of good conduct.
And how, Kuṇḍaliya, is restraint of the sense faculties developed, and how is it cultivated so that it fulfills the three types of good conduct? [The Buddha then proceeds to explain this in detail.]”
In this case, Kuṇḍaliya, when a bhikkhu sees a form with the eye, he does not covet what is pleasing, does not feel aversion toward it, and does not give rise to lust.
His body remains steady, and his mind remains steady—well-composed and well-liberated within.
Moreover, when he sees a form with the eye that is unpleasing, he is not dejected; his mind is not unsettled, his heart is not depressed, and his consciousness is not corrupted.
His body is steady and his mind is steady, well-composed and well-liberated within.
Furthermore, Kuṇḍaliya, having heard a sound with the ear...
having smelled an odor with the nose... [and so on].
Having tasted a flavor with the tongue …pe… having touched a tangible object with the body …pe… having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind,
one does not covet what is agreeable, does not harm it, and does not generate lust.
His body is steady, and his mind is steady within, well-composed and well-liberated.

Furthermore, having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind that is disagreeable, he does not become dejected; his mind is unestablished [in that], his disposition is undepressed, and his heart is free from malice.
His body is steady, and his mind is steady within, well-composed and well-liberated.

"Kundaliya, when a bhikkhu, having seen a form with the eye, remains with his body steady and his mind steady, well-composed and well-liberated within, regarding forms that are pleasant or unpleasant;
and when, having heard a sound with the ear...
[and so on] ...having smelled an odor with the nose..."
Having tasted a flavor with the tongue...
having touched a tangible object with the body...
having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, his body remains steady, and his mind—steadfast, well-composed, and well-liberated—remains within.
"Kundaliya, when the restraint of the sense faculties is thus developed and thus cultivated, it fulfills the three types of good conduct.
And how, Kundaliya, are the three types of good conduct developed and how are they cultivated so that they fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness?

Here, Kundaliya, a bhikkhu, having abandoned bodily misconduct, develops bodily good conduct; having abandoned verbal misconduct, he develops verbal good conduct; having abandoned mental misconduct, he develops mental good conduct."
“Thus, Kuṇḍaliya, when the three kinds of good conduct are developed and frequently practiced in this way, they fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness.
And how, Kuṇḍaliya, are the four foundations of mindfulness developed and frequently practiced so that they fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment?
Here, Kuṇḍaliya, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.”
He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings … mind in mind … phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
“Kuṇḍaliya, when the four foundations of mindfulness are developed in this way and cultivated in this way, they fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment.
And how, Kuṇḍaliya, are the seven factors of enlightenment developed and cultivated so that they fulfill true knowledge and liberation?

Here, Kuṇḍaliya, a bhikkhu develops the mindfulness factor of enlightenment dependent on seclusion, dependent on dispassion, dependent on cessation, resulting in relinquishment… [and so on for the remaining six factors]….”
“He develops the enlightenment factor of equanimity, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment.
It is when the seven factors of enlightenment have been developed and cultivated in this way, Kuṇḍaliya, that they fulfill true knowledge and liberation.
When this was said, the wanderer Kuṇḍaliya addressed the Blessed One as follows:
“Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent, Master Gotama!

Just as, Master Gotama, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—just so has Master Gotama made the Dhamma clear in many ways.”
"In this very way, the Venerable Gotama has proclaimed the Dhamma in many ways.
I go for refuge to the Venerable Gotama, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
May the Venerable Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last."

2. Gilānavagga. First Discourse on the Sick.
At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Now at that time, the Venerable Mahākassapa was staying in the Pippali Cave, afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill.
Then, in the evening, the Blessed One emerged from seclusion and approached the Venerable Mahākassapa.
Having approached, he sat down on the prepared seat. Once seated, the Blessed One said this to the Venerable Mahākassapa:
“Is it bearable for you, Kassapa? Is it sustainable? Are the painful feelings subsiding and not increasing? Is their subsiding apparent, and not their increase? “It is not bearable for me, Bhante;
it is not sustainable. My painful feelings are intense; they are increasing and not subsiding. Their increase is apparent, and not their subsiding.
“Kassapa, these seven factors of enlightenment have been rightly expounded by me; when developed and cultivated, they lead to direct knowledge, to full awakening, and to Nibbāna.”
Which seven?
The factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness, Kassapa, has been rightly expounded by me; when developed and cultivated, it leads to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, and to Nibbāna...

[and so on] ...the factor of enlightenment that is equanimity, Kassapa, has been rightly expounded by me; when developed and cultivated, it leads to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, and to Nibbāna.
“When developed and cultivated, it leads to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, and to Nibbāna.
Kassapa, these seven factors of enlightenment have been rightly expounded by me; when developed and cultivated, they lead to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, and to Nibbāna.
“Truly, Blessed One, they are the factors of enlightenment!”
“Truly, O Sugata, they are factors of enlightenment.
This is what the Blessed One said.
The Venerable Mahākassapa, being uplifted, rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
And the Venerable Mahākassapa recovered from that illness.
Thus was that illness abandoned by the Venerable Mahākassapa.
The fourth [sutta].

The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is sick, he should be attended to by a companion bhikkhu in five ways. What five? (4) He should attend to him with regard to his robes. (5) He should encourage him to reflect upon the Dhamma. When a bhikkhu is sick, he should be attended to by a companion bhikkhu in these five ways. This is what the Blessed One said. The Sutta on the Basis:
“Bhikkhus, through frequent attention to things that are the basis for sensual lust, unarisen sensual desire arises and arisen sensual desire leads to its increase and expansion.
Through frequent attention to things that are the basis for ill will, unarisen ill will arises and arisen ill will leads to its increase and expansion.”
“Bhikkhus, by frequently giving attention to things that are the basis for sloth and torpor, unarisen sloth and torpor arise, and arisen sloth and torpor increase and expand.
By frequently giving attention to things that are the basis for restlessness and remorse, unarisen restlessness and remorse arise, and arisen restlessness and remorse increase and expand.”
“Bhikkhus, by frequently attending to states that are the basis for doubt, unarisen doubt arises and arisen doubt increases and expands.

By frequently attending to states that are the basis for the enlightenment factor of mindfulness, the unarisen enlightenment factor of mindfulness arises and the arisen enlightenment factor of mindfulness reaches fulfillment by development … [and so on] …”

“By giving frequent attention to those things that are the basis for the enlightenment factor of equanimity, monks, the unarisen enlightenment factor of equanimity arises, and the arisen enlightenment factor of equanimity reaches fulfillment by development.
Thus it was said. The third [discourse]. *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 46.24. (SN 46.24, PTS SN v 84)
3. Udāyivagga:

The Discourse on Unwise Attention “Bhikkhus, for one who attends unwise attention, sensual desire that has not yet arisen arises, and sensual desire that has already arisen leads to its increase and expansion.
Ill will that has not yet arisen arises, and ill will that has already arisen leads to its increase and expansion;
sloth and torpor that have not yet arisen arise, and sloth and torpor that have already arisen lead to their increase and expansion;
restlessness and remorse that have not yet arisen arise, and restlessness and remorse that have already arisen lead to their increase and expansion.
Doubt that has not yet arisen arises, and doubt that has already arisen leads to increase and expansion.

The enlightenment factor of mindfulness that has not yet arisen does not arise, and the enlightenment factor of mindfulness that has already arisen ceases... [and so on] ...the enlightenment factor of equanimity that has not yet arisen does not arise, and the enlightenment factor of equanimity that has already arisen ceases.
But for one who attends wisely, monks, sensual desire that has not yet arisen does not arise, and sensual desire that has already arisen is abandoned.
Unarisen ill will does not arise, and arisen ill will is abandoned;
unarisen sloth and torpor do not arise, and arisen sloth and torpor are abandoned;
unarisen restlessness and remorse do not arise, and arisen restlessness and remorse are abandoned.
Doubt that has not yet arisen does not arise, and doubt that has already arisen is abandoned.

The enlightenment factor of mindfulness that has not yet arisen arises, and the enlightenment factor of mindfulness that has already arisen reaches fulfillment through development …pe… the enlightenment factor of equanimity that has not yet arisen arises, and the enlightenment factor of equanimity that has already arisen [reaches fulfillment].
“...the development reaches fulfillment. Thus it was said.
The fourth [discourse].
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 46.25 (SN 46.25, PTS SN v 85).
3. Udāyivagga Aparihāniyasutta:
“Bhikkhus, I will teach you seven principles that lead to non-decline.”
Listen to that.
And what, bhikkhus, are the seven qualities that prevent decline?
That is to say:
The seven factors of enlightenment.
Which seven?
The mindfulness factor of enlightenment …pe… the equanimity factor of enlightenment.
“Monks, these are the seven qualities that prevent decline.
Thus was the fifth [discourse]. *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 46.26 (SN 46.26, PTS SN v 86).
3. Udāyivagga:
Taṇhakkhayasutta “Bhikkhus, cultivate that path and that way of practice which leads to the destruction of craving.”
And what, monks, is the path and what is the practice that leads to the destruction of craving?
That is to say:
the seven factors of enlightenment.
“What seven?
The mindfulness factor of enlightenment … [and so on] … the equanimity factor of enlightenment.
When this was said, the Venerable Udāyī said this to the Blessed One:
“How, venerable sir, are the seven factors of enlightenment developed and cultivated so that they lead to the destruction of craving?

“Here, Udāyi, a bhikkhu develops the mindfulness factor of enlightenment, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment; it is vast, exalted, measureless, and free from ill will. He develops the investigation-of-states factor of enlightenment… the energy factor of enlightenment… the rapture factor of enlightenment… the tranquility factor of enlightenment… the concentration factor of enlightenment… the equanimity factor of enlightenment, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment; it is vast, exalted, measureless, and free from ill will.”

As he develops the mindfulness factor of enlightenment, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment—vast, exalted, immeasurable, and free from ill will—craving is abandoned.
With the abandoning of craving, karma is abandoned.
With the abandoning of karma, suffering is abandoned... [and so on].

He develops the factor of enlightenment that is equanimity, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment—vast, exalted, immeasurable, and free from ill will.

As he develops this factor of enlightenment that is equanimity, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment—vast, exalted, immeasurable, and free from ill will—craving is abandoned;
with the abandoning of craving, karma is abandoned.
“With the abandoning of karma, suffering is abandoned.
Thus, Udāyi, through the destruction of craving comes the destruction of karma; through the destruction of karma comes the destruction of suffering.
The sixth.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 46.27 (SN 46.27, PTS SN v 87) 3. Udāyivagga Taṇhānirodhasutta (The Discourse on the Cessation of Craving) At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, craving ceases with the cessation of what? With the cessation of feeling, craving ceases. With the cessation of contact, feeling ceases. With the cessation of the sixfold base, contact ceases. With the cessation of name-and-form, the sixfold base ceases. With the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases. With the cessation of formations, consciousness ceases. With the cessation of ignorance, formations cease. “Bhikkhus, when ignorance is abandoned and true knowledge has arisen, then with the fading away of ignorance and the arising of true knowledge, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases; with the cessation of birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease. Such is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.”
“Monks, cultivate that path and that way of practice which leads to the cessation of craving.
And what, monks, is that path and what is that way of practice which leads to the cessation of craving?
It is this:”
There are seven factors of enlightenment. Which seven?
The mindfulness factor of enlightenment …pe… the equanimity factor of enlightenment.
"And how, bhikkhus, are the seven factors of enlightenment developed and cultivated so as to lead to the cessation of craving?
Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu develops the mindfulness factor of enlightenment dependent on seclusion, dependent on dispassion, dependent on cessation, resulting in relinquishment...
[and so on for the remaining factors] ...he develops the equanimity factor of enlightenment dependent on seclusion, dependent on dispassion, dependent on cessation, resulting in relinquishment."
“Monks, when the seven factors of enlightenment are thus developed and cultivated in this way, they lead to the cessation of craving.
The seventh. Saṃyutta Nikāya 46.28.
3. Udāyivagga Nibbedhabhāgiyasutta “Bhikkhus, I will teach you the path that partakes of penetration. Listen to it.”
Listen to that.
And what, bhikkhus, is the path partaking of penetration?
It is this: namely—
There are seven factors of enlightenment. Which seven?
The mindfulness factor of enlightenment … [and so on] … the equanimity factor of enlightenment.
When this was said, the Venerable Udāyī addressed the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, how are the seven factors of enlightenment developed and cultivated so that they lead to penetration?

“Here, Udāyī, a bhikkhu develops the mindfulness factor of enlightenment, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment; it is vast, exalted, immeasurable, and free from ill will. He develops the investigation-of-phenomena factor of enlightenment… the energy factor of enlightenment… the rapture factor of enlightenment… the tranquility factor of enlightenment… the concentration factor of enlightenment… the equanimity factor of enlightenment, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment; it is vast, exalted, immeasurable, and free from ill will.”
Thus, with a mind developed through the enlightenment factor of mindfulness, he pierces and shatters the mass of greed never before pierced or shattered;
he pierces and shatters the mass of hatred never before pierced or shattered;
he pierces and shatters the mass of delusion never before pierced or shattered... [and so on].

He develops the factor of enlightenment that is equanimity, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment—vast, exalted, immeasurable, and free from ill will.
With his mind developed in this factor of enlightenment of equanimity, he pierces and shatters the mass of greed never before pierced or shattered;
he pierces and shatters the mass of hatred never before pierced or shattered.
He pierces and shatters the mass of delusion that has never before been pierced and never before shattered.
It is when the seven factors of enlightenment are thus developed and cultivated in this way, Udāyi, that they lead to penetration.
The eighth.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 46.29 (SN 46.29, PTS SN v 88) 3. Udāyivagga Ekadhammasutta “Monks, there is one thing which, when developed and cultivated, leads to the abandoning of all unwholesome states. What is that one thing? Mindfulness directed to the body. This is that one thing, monks, which, when developed and cultivated, leads to the abandoning of all unwholesome states.”
“Bhikkhus, I do not see even a single other thing that, when developed and cultivated, leads to the abandoning of the things that fetter as much as these seven factors of enlightenment.
What seven?
The mindfulness factor of enlightenment … [and so on] … the equanimity factor of enlightenment.”
And how, monks, are the seven factors of enlightenment developed and cultivated so as to lead to the abandoning of the things that fetter?
Here, monks, a monk develops the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness, based on seclusion...
[and so on] ...he develops the factor of enlightenment that is equanimity, based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, resulting in relinquishment.
"Monks, when the seven factors of enlightenment are thus developed and cultivated in this way, they lead to the abandoning of the things that fetter.
And what, monks, are the things that fetter?
The eye, monks, is a thing that fetters."
Herein these fetters, bondages, and attachments arise … [as before] … the tongue is a phenomenon that fetters.
Herein these fetters, bondages, and attachments arise … [as before] …
“Mind is a phenomenon that fetters.
Herein, these fetters, bondages, and attachments arise.
These, monks, are called the phenomena that fetter.”
The Ninth.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 46.30 (SN 46.30, PTS SN v 89) 3. Udāyivagga
The Udāyī Sutta.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sumbhas at a town of the Sumbhas named Setaka.
Then the Venerable Udāyī approached the Blessed One... [and] sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Udāyī said this to the Blessed One:
“It is wonderful, Bhante! It is marvelous, Bhante!
To such an extent, Bhante, have I performed much service for the Blessed One, and possess love, reverence, moral shame, and moral dread toward him.
For formerly, when I was still a householder, I had not performed much service for the Dhamma, nor had I performed much service for the Saṅgha.”
Thus, perceiving love, reverence, moral shame, and moral dread toward the Blessed One, I went forth from the home life into homelessness.
To me, the Blessed One taught the Dhamma:
"Such is form, such is the arising of form, such is the passing away of form."
Thus is feeling … [and so on] … thus is perception … thus are volitional formations …
‘Such is consciousness, such is the arising of consciousness, such is the passing away of consciousness.
Then, venerable sir, having gone to an empty place and turning these five aggregates of clinging over and over again, righting them and overturning them, I directly knew as it really is:
‘This is suffering,’ and I directly knew as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering.’
‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ I directly knew as it really is; ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering,’ I directly knew as it really is.
And the Dhamma has been realized by me, venerable sir, and the path has been attained by me;
"That factor of enlightenment which, when developed and cultivated by me, will lead me—who dwells accordingly—to suchness, so that I may understand:

‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being’—that factor of enlightenment called mindfulness has been attained by me, venerable sir, which, when developed and cultivated by me, will lead me—who dwells accordingly—to suchness, so that I may understand: [the same as above].”
“I shall understand: ‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
… [as before] … Venerable sir, the enlightenment factor of equanimity has been acquired by me; when developed and cultivated, it will lead me to such a state that I shall understand:
‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.’”
“Bhante, this is the path I have attained; when developed and cultivated by me, dwelling in such a way, it will lead me to suchness that I shall understand:
‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
“Excellent, excellent, Udāyin!”
"For this, Udāyin, is the path you have found; when developed and cultivated by you, it will lead one who dwells accordingly toward suchness, so that you will understand:
'Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
This is the tenth [sutta].
The third chapter is the Udāyi-vagga.
Its summary verse (uddāna) is:
"The teaching for enlightenment, the grounds..."
And lack of careful attention leads to decline;
destruction, cessation, and penetration—
this is the one thing, Udāyin.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 46.31 4. Nīvaraṇavagga First Discourse on the Wholesome "Bhikkhus, there are these five hindrances. What five? The hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, and the hindrance of doubt. These, bhikkhus, are the five hindrances. And what, bhikkhus, is the wholesome? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu develops the basis for psychic power that possesses concentration due to desire and volitional formations of striving; he develops the basis for psychic power that possesses concentration due to energy and volitional formations of striving; he develops the basis for psychic power that possesses concentration due to mind and volitional formations of striving; he develops the basis for psychic power that possesses concentration due to investigation and volitional formations of striving. This, bhikkhus, is called the wholesome. Thus, bhikkhus, having abandoned the unwholesome and cultivated the wholesome, having abandoned the hindrances and cultivated the wholesome, a bhikkhu should dwell with a mind well-restrained by mindfulness."

“Bhikkhus, whatever states are wholesome, partaking of the wholesome, and belonging to the side of the wholesome—all these have heedfulness as their root and converge upon heedfulness; heedfulness is declared to be the foremost of those states.
For a bhikkhu who is heedful, bhikkhus, this is to be expected: he will develop the seven factors of enlightenment and cultivate them frequently.
And how, bhikkhus, does a bhikkhu who is heedful develop the seven factors of enlightenment and cultivate them frequently?”
"Here, monks, a monk develops the mindfulness factor of enlightenment dependent on seclusion...
[and so on] ...he develops the equanimity factor of enlightenment dependent on seclusion, dependent on fading away, dependent on cessation, resulting in relinquishment.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk who is diligent develops the seven factors of enlightenment and cultivates the seven factors of enlightenment."
First.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 46.32 (SN 46.32, PTS SN v 91) 4.
The Chapter on Hindrances (Nīvaraṇavagga)

The Second Discourse on the Wholesome “Bhikkhus, whatever states are wholesome, partaking of the wholesome, and belonging to the side of the wholesome—all these have wise attention as their root and converge upon wise attention. Wise attention is declared to be the foremost of those states.
For a bhikkhu endowed with wise attention, it is to be expected that he will develop the seven factors of enlightenment and cultivate the seven factors of enlightenment repeatedly.”
And how, monks, does a monk endowed with wise attention develop the seven factors of awakening and cultivate the seven factors of awakening?
Here, monks, a monk develops the mindfulness factor of awakening based on seclusion...
[and so on] ...he develops the equanimity factor of awakening based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, resulting in relinquishment.
“It is in this way, monks, that a monk endowed with wise attention develops the seven factors of awakening and cultivates the seven factors of awakening.
The second.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 46.33.
4. The Chapter on Hindrances:

The Discourse on Defilements “Monks, there are these five defilements of gold, by which defiled gold is neither malleable nor wieldy, nor is it luminous and brittle; it does not properly serve for work.
What are the five?
Iron, bhikkhus, is an impurity of gold; when gold is defiled by this impurity, it is neither soft nor workable, nor is it radiant and malleable, and it does not properly lend itself to being worked.
Copper, bhikkhus, is an impurity of gold; when gold is defiled by this impurity... [and so on].
“Monks, dross is an impurity of gold... monks, lead is an impurity of gold... monks, copper is an impurity of gold.
When gold is defiled by such impurities, it is neither soft nor workable, nor is it radiant; it is brittle and does not properly lend itself to being worked.”
“Monks, these are the five impurities of gold, by which impurities defiled,
gold is neither soft nor workable, nor is it radiant and malleable;
it does not properly lend itself to being worked.”
In the same way, monks, there are these five defilements of the mind; by these defilements, when the mind is defiled,
it is neither pliant nor wieldy, nor is it luminous and malleable,
and it does not become rightly concentrated for the destruction of the taints.
Which five?
Sensual desire, monks, is a defilement of the mind;
by this defilement, when the mind is defiled, it is neither pliant nor wieldy, neither luminous nor malleable, and it does not become rightly concentrated.
For the destruction of the taints...
These, monks, are the five defilements of the mind;
when the mind is defiled by these defilements, it is neither pliant nor wieldy, nor is it luminous and malleable, and it does not become rightly concentrated.
“...for the destruction of the taints.
The third.
*Saṁyutta Nikāya* 46.34. (SN 46.34, PTS SN v 93)
4. The Chapter on Hindrances:

The Discourse on Lack of Corruptions “Bhikkhus, these seven factors of enlightenment, when developed and cultivated, are unobstructed, unhindered, and free from corruptions of the mind; they lead to the realization of the fruit of true knowledge and liberation.”
Which seven?
Monks, the mindfulness factor of enlightenment is unobstructed, unimpeded, and untainted by mental defilements;
when developed and cultivated extensively, it leads to the realization of the fruit of true knowledge and liberation. … [and so on] … monks, the equanimity factor of enlightenment is unobstructed.
“Unobstructed, unobstructing, and undefiled by the mind, when developed and cultivated extensively, this leads to the realization of the fruit of true knowledge and liberation.

These, monks, are the seven factors of enlightenment that—unobstructed, unobstructing, and undefiled by the mind—are developed and cultivated extensively, leading to the realization of the fruit of true knowledge and liberation.
This was the fourth [discourse].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 46.35 (SN 46.35, PTS SN v 93) 4. The Chapter on Hindrances (Nīvaraṇavagga) The Discourse on Unwise Attention (Ayonisomanasikārasutta) “Bhikkhus, unwise attention is the root of the unwholesome; wise attention is the root of the wholesome. And what, bhikkhus, is unwise attention? ‘This is suffering’—to attend to this not wisely; ‘This is the origin of suffering’—to attend to this not wisely; ‘This is the cessation of suffering’—to attend to this not wisely; ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’—to attend to this not wisely. This, bhikkhus, is called unwise attention. And what, bhikkhus, is wise attention? ‘This is suffering’—to attend to this wisely; ‘This is the origin of suffering’—to attend to this wisely; ‘This is the cessation of suffering’—to attend to this wisely; ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’—to attend to this wisely. This, bhikkhus, is called wise attention.”
“Bhikkhus, for one who attends to things improperly, unarisen sensual desire arises, and arisen sensual desire leads to its increase and expansion;
unarisen ill will arises, and arisen ill will leads to its increase and expansion; unarisen sloth and torpor arise... [and so on].”
Unarisen sloth and torpor arise, and arisen sloth and torpor lead to their increase and expansion;
unarisen restlessness and remorse arise, and arisen restlessness and remorse lead to their increase and expansion;
unarisen doubt arises, and arisen doubt leads to its increase and expansion.
“...it leads to expansion.
The fifth:
*Yonisomanasikārasutta*.
“Monks, for one who attends wisely, the enlightenment factor of mindfulness that has not yet arisen arises,
and the enlightenment factor of mindfulness that has already arisen reaches fulfillment through development … [and so on] … the enlightenment factor of equanimity that has not yet arisen arises,
and the enlightenment factor of equanimity that has already arisen reaches fulfillment through development.”
Sixth. Saṁyutta Nikāya 46.36 (SN 46.36, PTS SN v 94) 4.
The Chapter on Hindrances (Nīvaraṇavagga)
The Discourse on Awakening:
“Bhikkhus, these seven factors of awakening, when developed and cultivated, lead to the non-decline of wisdom.
Which seven?”
The enlightenment factor of mindfulness … [and so on] … the enlightenment factor of equanimity.
These seven factors of enlightenment, bhikkhus, when developed and cultivated, lead to non-decline in wisdom. Thus it was said.
The seventh [sutta].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 46.37 (SN 46.37, PTS SN v 94) 4. The Chapter on Hindrances (Nīvaraṇavagga) The Discourse on Obstruction and Hindrance (Āvaraṇanīvaraṇasutta) “Bhikkhus, there are these five hindrances. What five? The hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, and the hindrance of doubt.
These, bhikkhus, are the five hindrances.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these five hindrances, obstructions, defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom.
Which five?
Sensual desire, bhikkhus, is an obstruction, an impediment, a defilement of the mind that weakens wisdom.”
Ill will, monks, is an obstruction, a hindrance, a defilement of the mind, a weakening of wisdom.
Sloth and torpor, monks, are an obstruction, a hindrance, a defilement of the mind, a weakening of wisdom.
Restlessness and remorse, monks, are an obstruction, a hindrance, a defilement of the mind, a weakening of wisdom.
“Bhikkhus, doubt is an obstruction, a hindrance, a defilement of the mind, a weakening of wisdom.
These, bhikkhus, are the five obstructions, hindrances, defilements of the mind, weakeners of wisdom.

“There are, bhikkhus, these seven factors of enlightenment that are non-obstructions, non-hindrances, non-defilements of the mind; when developed and cultivated, they lead to the realization of the fruit of true knowledge and liberation.”
Which seven?
Monks, the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness is unobstructed, unimpeded, and untainted by defilements of the mind;
when developed and cultivated extensively, it leads to the realization of the fruit of true knowledge and liberation. …pe… Monks, the factor of enlightenment that is equanimity is unobstructed.
Unobstructed, unclouded, and free from mental defilement, when developed and cultivated extensively, it leads to the realization of the fruit of true knowledge and liberation.

These, monks, are the seven factors of enlightenment that—unobstructed, unclouded, and free from mental defilement—when developed and cultivated extensively, lead to the realization of the fruit of true knowledge and liberation.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya 46.38 (SN 46.38, PTS SN v 95)*
4. The Chapter on Hindrances:
The Discourse on Being Without Hindrances “Bhikkhus, at whatever time a noble disciple, having made it his bone, having attended to it, and having applied his whole mind, [practices]...”
When one listens to the Dhamma with attentive ears, at that time the five hindrances do not exist for him.
At that time, the seven factors of enlightenment reach fulfillment through development.
Which five hindrances do not exist at that time?
At that time, the hindrance of sensual desire does not exist; at that time, the hindrance of ill will does not exist;
at that time, the hindrance of sloth and torpor does not exist; at that time, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse does not exist;
at that time, the hindrance of doubt does not exist.
At that time, these five hindrances do not exist.
Which seven factors of enlightenment reach fulfillment through cultivation at that time?
At that time, the mindfulness factor of enlightenment reaches fulfillment through cultivation …pe… at that time, the equanimity factor of enlightenment reaches fulfillment through cultivation.
At that time, these seven factors of enlightenment reach fulfillment through development.

Monks, at whatever time a noble disciple listens to the Dhamma with intentness, having made it his bone, having made it his mind, having applied his whole heart, and lending an attentive ear, at that time the five hindrances do not exist for him. These seven...
“On that occasion, the factors of enlightenment reach fulfillment by development.
The eighth.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 46.39 (SN 46.39, PTS SN v 96)
4. The Chapter on Hindrances:

The Discourse on Trees “Monks, there are great trees with minute seeds that grow into massive trunks and climb over other trees; and because they have climbed over them, those trees lie broken, shattered, and fallen.”

"And what, monks, are those great trees that have small seeds and become large-bodied, climbing upon other trees, by which the trees they have climbed are broken down, shattered, and lie fallen? The *assattha*, the *nigrodha*,
the *pilakkha*, the *udumbara*, the *kacchaka*, and the *kapitthana*— these, monks,
are those great trees with small seeds that become large-bodied, climbing upon other trees, by which the trees they have climbed are broken down, shattered, and lie fallen."

"In the same way, monks, here a certain clansman, having abandoned such sensual pleasures as he left home for the homeless life, lies broken, shattered, and fallen away from those very same sensual pleasures, or from even worse ones.
Monks, there are these five hindrances, obstructions, mental obsessions that weaken wisdom.
What are the five?"
Sensual desire, monks, is an obstruction, a hindrance, an encroachment upon the mind, and a weakening of wisdom.
Ill will, monks, is an obstruction, a hindrance, an encroachment upon the mind, and a weakening of wisdom.
Sloth and torpor, monks, are an obstruction, a hindrance, an encroachment upon the mind, and a weakening of wisdom.
Restlessness and remorse, monks, are an obstruction, a hindrance, an encroachment upon the mind, and a weakening of wisdom.
Doubt, monks, is an obstruction, a hindrance, an encroachment upon the mind, and a weakening of wisdom.
These, monks, are the five obstructions, hindrances, encroachments upon the mind, and weakeners of wisdom.

"Bhikkhus, these seven factors of enlightenment are unobstructed, unimpeded, and do not lie heavy upon the mind; when developed and cultivated, they lead to the realization of the fruit of true knowledge and liberation.
What seven?
The factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, bhikkhus, is unobstructed, unimpeded, and does not lie heavy upon the mind; when developed and cultivated..."

“It leads to the realization of the fruit of true knowledge and liberation... Monks, the enlightenment factor of equanimity, when developed and cultivated—unobstructed, unimpeded, and not ascended upon by the mind—leads to the realization of the fruit of true knowledge and liberation.

These, monks, are the seven factors of enlightenment that, when developed and cultivated—unobstructed, unimpeded, and not ascended upon by the mind—lead to the realization of the fruit of true knowledge and liberation.”
The Ninth.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 46.40 (SN 46.40, PTS SN v 97) 4.
The Chapter on Hindrances (Nīvaraṇavagga)
The Discourse on the Hindrances:
“Bhikkhus, there are these five hindrances that cause blindness, cause lack of vision, cause lack of knowledge; they obstruct wisdom, belong to the side of affliction, and do not lead to Nibbāna.
Which five?”

“Bhikkhus, the hindrance of sensual desire makes for blindness, makes for lack of vision, makes for lack of knowledge; it obstructs wisdom, belongs to the side of affliction, and does not lead to Nibbāna.
The hindrance of ill will, bhikkhus … the hindrance of sloth and torpor, bhikkhus …” [and so forth].

“Bhikkhus, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse … the hindrance of doubt, bhikkhus, makes for blindness, makes for lack of vision, makes for lack of knowledge; it obstructs wisdom, belongs to the side of affliction, and does not lead to Nibbāna.

‘The hindrance of restlessness and remorse’—this is how it is designated here. By this method, it becomes twofold:
whatever doubt there is regarding internal phenomena, that too is a hindrance; whatever doubt there is regarding external phenomena, that too is a hindrance.
‘The hindrance of doubt’—this is how it is designated here. By this method, it also becomes twofold.
This, monks, is the method by which, depending on that method, the five hindrances become ten.
And what, monks, is the method by which, depending on that method, the seven factors of enlightenment become fourteen?

Whatever mindfulness there is, monks, regarding internal phenomena, that too is the mindfulness factor of enlightenment; whatever mindfulness there is regarding external phenomena, that too is the mindfulness factor of enlightenment.
‘The enlightenment factor of mindfulness’—this is how it is designated here. By this method, it becomes twofold:
that which, monks, discriminates, investigates, and enters upon examination with wisdom regarding internal phenomena is the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor;
and that which discriminates, investigates, and [enters upon examination] with wisdom regarding external phenomena...
To engage in thorough investigation—this too is the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena.
Thus, this is included under the summary term “enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena. By this method, there are two [types]:
monks, whatever is bodily energy, that too is the enlightenment factor of energy; whatever is mental energy, that too is the enlightenment factor of energy.
‘The enlightenment factor of energy’—this is how it comes under the heading. By this method, there are two kinds:

that which is rapture accompanied by directed thought and evaluation is the enlightenment factor of rapture, and that which is rapture without directed thought and evaluation is also the enlightenment factor of rapture.
‘The enlightenment factor of rapture’—this is how it comes under the heading. By this method, there are two kinds.
“Monks, whatever is tranquility of body is the enlightenment factor of tranquility; whatever is tranquility of mind is also the enlightenment factor of tranquility.
Thus, it is designated here as ‘the enlightenment factor of tranquility. By this method, there are two aspects to it.

Monks, whatever concentration is accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought is the enlightenment factor of concentration; whatever concentration is without applied thought and without sustained thought is also the enlightenment factor of concentration.”
‘The enlightenment factor of concentration’—this is how it is designated here. By this method, it becomes twofold:

whatever equanimity there is toward internal phenomena, that is the enlightenment factor of equanimity; whatever equanimity there is toward external phenomena, that too is the enlightenment factor of equanimity.
‘The enlightenment factor of equanimity’—this is how it is designated here. By this method, it becomes twofold.
“This, monks, is the method by which, relying on this method, the seven factors of enlightenment become fourteen.
The second.

But on whatever occasion, monks, the mind is sluggish, at that time it is the right time for the development of the investigation-of-phenomena factor of enlightenment,
the right time for the development of the energy factor of enlightenment, and the right time for the development of the rapture factor of enlightenment. Why is that?
“Bhikkhus, a sunken mind is easily raised up by these qualities.

“Yes, venerable sir.”—
“In the same way, bhikkhus, when the mind is sluggish, that is the time for the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena.”
It is the time for the cultivation of the energy enlightenment factor; it is the time for the cultivation of the rapture enlightenment factor.
Why is that? Because, monks, a sluggish mind is easily uplifted by these states.

“Bhikkhus, on whatever occasion the mind is agitated, that is not the time for the development of the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor, not the time for the development of the energy enlightenment factor, and not the time for the development of the rapture enlightenment factor. Why is that?
[Because the mind is already over-excitiated.]”
"Monks, an agitated mind is difficult to pacify by means of these things.
It is just as if, monks, a man were desirous of extinguishing a great mass of fire.
He would throw dry grass into it, he would throw dry cow dung into it, he would throw dry wood into it, he would blow on it with his mouth, and he would not sprinkle it with dust."
“Would that man be able, bhikkhus, to extinguish a great mass of fire?
“No indeed, venerable sir.
“In the same way, bhikkhus, when the mind is agitated, that is not the time [for the development of concentration].”
It is the time for the development of the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena, but it is not the time for the development of the enlightenment factor of energy,
nor is it the time for the development of the enlightenment factor of rapture. Why is that?
“Monks, an agitated mind is difficult to pacify by means of these states.

the time for the cultivation of the concentration factor of enlightenment, and the time for the cultivation of the equanimity factor of enlightenment.”
For what reason?
Because, monks, an agitated mind is easily pacified by these qualities.
It is just as if, monks, a man were desirous of extinguishing a great mass of fire.
“Suppose, in that case, one were to throw fresh grass into it, throw fresh cow dung into it, throw fresh wood into it, provide it with water and air, and sprinkle it with dust—

“Yes, venerable sir.”

“In the same way, monks, at whatever time the mind is agitated, that is the time for the development of the tranquility factor of enlightenment, the time for the development of the concentration factor of enlightenment, and the time for the development of the equanimity factor of enlightenment. “Bhikkhus, an excited mind is easily calmed by these qualities.
And mindfulness, bhikkhus, I call the all-beneficial. Thus was the third [sutta].

How, monks, is the liberation of mind through loving-kindness developed, what is its destination, what is its supreme state, what is its fruit, and what is its consummation?
Here, monks, a monk develops the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness accompanied by loving-kindness... [and so on].
He develops the enlightenment factor of equanimity accompanied by loving-kindness, based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and resulting in relinquishment.
If he wishes, "May I dwell perceiving the repulsive in the unrepulsive," he dwells there perceiving the repulsive.
If he wishes, "May I dwell perceiving the unrepulsive in the repulsive," he dwells there perceiving the unrepulsive.
If he wishes, “May I dwell perceiving the repulsive in both the repulsive and the non-repulsive,” he dwells there perceiving the repulsive.
If he wishes, “May I dwell perceiving the non-repulsive in both the repulsive and the non-repulsive,” he dwells there perceiving the non-repulsive.
If he wishes, “Avoiding both the repulsive and the non-repulsive, may I dwell in equanimity...”
‘Mindful and clearly comprehending’: he dwells there equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending; or else, having attained the beautiful liberation, he dwells therein.
Monks, for a monk here who possesses wisdom but has not yet penetrated higher liberation, I say that the liberation of mind through loving-kindness has beauty as its supreme limit.
"And how, bhikkhus, is the liberation of mind through compassion developed, what is its destination, what is its supreme state, what is its fruit, and what is its consummation? Here, bhikkhus,

“Bhikkhus, for a wise bhikkhu who has not penetrated to a higher liberation here and now, I say that the liberation of mind through compassion has the base of infinite space as its limit.

Monks, for a monk here who possesses wisdom but has not yet penetrated further liberation, I say that the liberation of mind through gladness has the base of infinite consciousness as its limit.

"Here, monks, a bhikkhu develops the mindfulness enlightenment factor accompanied by equanimity, based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, resulting in relinquishment...

If he wishes, "May I dwell perceiving the repulsive in both the unrepulsive and the repulsive," he dwells there perceiving the repulsive.
If he wishes, "May I dwell perceiving the unrepulsive in both the repulsive and the unrepulsive," he dwells there perceiving the unrepulsive.

“If he should wish: ‘May I dwell equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending, having turned away from both the unrepulsive and the repulsive,’ he dwells there equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending.
Or, by completely transcending the base of infinite consciousness, perceiving ‘there is nothing,’ he enters and dwells in the base of nothingness.
Monks, for a wise monk here who has not penetrated to a further liberation, I say that this deliverance of mind through equanimity has the base of nothingness as its limit.”

“Brahmin, on whatever occasion one dwells with a mind obsessed by sensual lust, dominated by sensual lust,
and does not understand as it really is the escape from arisen sensual lust—
at that time one neither knows nor sees one’s own welfare as it really is, nor at that time does one know or see the welfare of others as it really is.”
He knows but does not see; at that time, he neither knows nor sees things as they truly are in both respects.
Even mantras he has recited for a long time do not come to mind, let alone those he has not recited.
It is just as if, brahmin, there were a bowl of water mixed with lac, turmeric, indigo, or madder.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 46.58 (SN 46.58, PTS SN v 131) 7. Ānāpānavagga Puḷavakasutta (The Worm-Eaten) “Bhikkhus, suppose there were a worm-eaten log lying on a heap of leaves. A man with good eyesight, looking at it, would say: ‘This worm-eaten log lying on the heap of leaves is decaying; it is rotten inside, but not yet decayed outside. In the same way, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu’s mind is inwardly settled, quieted, unified, and concentrated, he knows: ‘My mind is inwardly settled, quieted, unified, and concentrated. When his mind is inwardly settled, quieted, unified, and concentrated, he applies it to the knowledge of the arising and passing away of phenomena. He understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. Just as that worm-eaten log was decaying inside though not yet decayed outside, so too, when a bhikkhu’s mind is inwardly settled… he understands as it really is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. This, bhikkhus, is called a bhikkhu who is like a worm-eaten log.”
“Monks, the perception of a worm-infested corpse, when developed …” The second [sutta].
